location_min_interval_ms is the least time, in milliseconds, between two fixes accepted from one beacon. The range is 0 to 60000 and the default is 250. A fix that arrives sooner than this after the previous accepted one is refused and counted as Rate limited on the beacon.

Zero disables the limit. A beacon can carry its own Min interval on its page, which overrides this sitewide value for that beacon alone; blank there uses this.

Use it to protect the system from a phone that posts far faster than the tracker can show. The accepted fixes are then subject to location_min_distance_m, which decides whether each is stored or only shown live.

label: Minimum fix distance
title: Which fixes get recorded
body:
location_min_distance_m decides which accepted fixes are stored as location rows. A fix that moved less than this many metres from the beacon's last recorded fix on the event is still published live to the tracker but is not recorded, and is counted as Carried on the beacon. The range is 0 to 10000, decimals allowed, and the default is 0.

At 0 every new position is recorded, but a position already recorded for the event, an exact repeat of latitude and longitude, is never recorded twice. A few metres keeps a parked sleigh from filling the event's Locations with identical rows.

Only recorded rows appear in the Locations card, the CSV, and a recording built from the event, so set this before the flight, not after.

label: Hub enabled
title: Live socket on or off
body:
hub_enabled is a switch, on by default. On, visitors' browsers connect to the hub, a live socket that pushes each new position the moment it arrives, with the poll as a fallback. Off, every visitor stops using the hub and relies on polling the CDN at the poll interval; the change takes every visitor onto the poll within one poll.

The switch saves the moment it is flipped. Turn it off if the hub misbehaves on the night; the tracker keeps working at the poll rate.

The switch covers visitors only. Whether a beacon may use the hub is its own Hub allowed switch on the beacon page, and the hub state chip there shows whether it is connected or polling.

label: Route map tolerance
title: Simplifying the route line
body:
route_map_simplify_tolerance_m is the tolerance, in metres, used to simplify a flight recording's path before the route map is smoothed and drawn. The range is 1 to 500 and the default is 30. Points that deviate from the straight line between their neighbours by less than this are dropped.

A larger tolerance gives a cleaner, lighter line and loses small wiggles; a smaller one keeps detail and more points. It applies to the route map in the snapshot, to the preview in the event page's route map dialog, and to posters, so all three draw the same line.

It is separate from flight_history_max_points, which thins the tracker's flight history. A change shows on the site's next snapshot.

label: Route map max points
title: Capping the route map path
body:
route_map_max_points is the most vertices the route map path may have after simplification. The range is 100 to 10000 and the default is 1200. When the simplified path still has more, it is thinned evenly, always keeping the first and last vertex.

The cap bounds how much path data the snapshot carries and how much work each browser does to draw it. It applies to the snapshot's route map, the event page's route map preview, and posters alike.

Raise it for a long flight whose line looks angular after simplification; lower it to keep the snapshot small. Tune route_map_simplify_tolerance_m first, since it decides how many points survive before this cap is applied. A change shows on the next snapshot.

label: Default route duration
title: Timing an untimed recording
body:
route_map_default_duration_minutes is the flight length assumed for a recording that has no usable times, meaning fewer than two timed points. The range is 10 to 720 and the default is 120. The duration is spread along the path by distance, so time labels and the route map's timeline can still be drawn.

A recording uploaded from a file with recordedAt set to null on its points, or built from a source without timestamps, falls into this case. A recording with real times ignores this value.

It affects the time labels in the event page's route map dialog and on posters, and the snapshot's route map. Set it close to the real flight length so the labels read sensibly. A change shows on the next snapshot.

label: API keys list
title: Keys for scripts and agents
body:
An API key lets a script or an agent configure the site through the API without signing in. This page, for admins only, lists every key with its name, prefix, a status chip of Active, Expired, or Revoked, chips for what it may do, the expiry, when it was last used, and who created it.

New key opens the create dialog. The key itself is shown once, in the same reveal dialog beacons use, and never again. The row menu holds Revoke, which asks for confirmation and stops anything using the key immediately.

Keys are hashed at rest, cannot create or revoke other keys, and skip the sign-in's second factor, so revoking is the only lasting control. The Agents page walks through using one for a session.

label: New key dialog
title: Creating an API key
body:
The dialog asks for a name of 1 to 100 characters, unique among keys. All capabilities is on by default and gives the key everything; turn it off to tick individual capabilities, at least one, from the list in the next topic.

Never expires is also on by default. Turn it off to set an expiry, which must be at least an hour ahead; an expired key stops working on its own and shows red in the list.

Create reveals the key once in a dialog that cannot be dismissed until you press I have stored the key. Copy it into the script or agent's configuration then and there. Prefer a short expiry and the fewest capabilities the job needs; revoke it when the job is done.

label: Capability list
title: What a key may touch
body:
Capabilities are the areas of the API a key may reach, one per area of the panel: Events, Flight recordings, Beacons, Sponsors, Cookie types, Pages, Sections, Site settings, Publish and versions, Media, Icons, Settings, Contact messages, Subscribers, People, Diagnostics, Audit, and QR codes and places.

A key with QR codes and places reaches the canvasser routes, including the deletes. No key can list, create, or revoke API keys or read the email quota; those need a signed-in admin.

Pick the smallest set that does the job: a content agent needs Pages, Sections, Media, Icons, and Publish and versions, not Events or Beacons. Capabilities are fixed at creation; to change them, revoke the key and create another.

label: Agents page
title: Running an agent for a session
body:
This admin-only page is the recipe for letting an agent, such as a coding assistant, or any script work on the site for one session. Four steps: mint a key with only the capabilities the job needs, hand the agent the key and the prompt, let it work, then revoke the key. Revocation is the only lasting control, because keys cannot mint or revoke keys and skip the sign-in's second factor.

The API keys list is mounted right here so minting and revoking happen in place.

Below it is the Agent prompt: a long plain-text guide to the API with a Copy button, covering authentication, conventions, every capability and its routes, the content model, delete safety, the media pipeline, the event lifecycle, common workflows, and the rules an agent must follow, such as never changing a status, publishing, or deleting unless asked.

label: Audit log
title: Who changed what, when
body:
The audit log records every write made through the panel or the API: creates, edits, deletes, status changes, publishes, seeded cookies, and more. Each row shows the time, who did it and the action, the entity and its id, and a summary of the fields that changed. Expand a row for the raw before and after.

The entity id links to the row's page for events, beacons, sponsors, pages, and QR codes, unless the entry is a delete. Deleted rows are readable here and nowhere else, so this is where to find what a deleted event or sponsor contained.

The list is newest first and loads more on demand. The same history is reachable per row through the Audit icon at the end of every list in the panel. Admins and editors can open this page.

label: Audit filters
title: Narrowing the audit log
body:
The filter paper has four controls. Entity picks the kind of thing, such as event, page, or setting, from the kinds the API has recorded. Action picks the verb, such as create, update, delete, or cookies_seeded. Actor filters by who made the change, an email or a key name. The Deletes chip is a shortcut that sets the action to delete.

Changing a filter reloads the list from the newest match. Combine them to answer a question such as which settings this person changed last week, or what was deleted this month.

The filters do not persist; opening the page again shows everything. On a phone the controls wrap onto their own lines.

label: Publish button
title: The Publish button in the bar
body:
The Publish button in the top bar appears only while the draft has changes that are not yet published, and only for admins and editors. When nothing is unpublished it is not there at all. On a phone it is an icon.

With no problems, a click opens the same label dialog as the Publish page: an optional label, and the reminder that the public site updates within its next poll. Confirming publishes from wherever you are, toasts the new version number, and the button disappears.

When the draft has problems the button carries a badge with the count, and a click opens the Publish page instead, where each problem links to the place to fix it. The panel checks the status every 30 seconds while the tab is visible.

label: Environment badge
title: Which site you are editing
body:
The badge in the top bar names the environment: PROD in red, DEV in green, or LOCAL in blue. PROD is the real public site and everything you do there is visible to visitors once published or, for events, beacons, and settings, at once. DEV is the development copy for trying things out.

Hovering the badge shows which API this panel talks to. On DEV and LOCAL the browser tab's title is also prefixed with the environment name, so a glance at the tab tells them apart.

The badge also appears on the sign-in and setup pages. Check it before changing an event status, seeding cookies, or revoking anything.

label: Navigation drawer
title: The left menu and roles
body:
The drawer on the left lists every page your role can open, in one flat list; the current page is highlighted. On a phone it hides behind the menu button in the bar.

What you see depends on your role. An admin sees everything: Dashboard, Events, Flight recordings, Beacons, QR codes, Places, Scan, Pages, Media, Poster studio, Site settings, Publish, Sponsors, Sponsor order, Cookie types, Subscribers, People, Contact messages, Settings, API keys, Agents, and Audit. An editor sees Pages, Media, Site settings, Publish, Sponsors, Sponsor order, QR codes, Places, Scan, and Audit. A canvasser sees QR codes, Places, and Scan, and lands on Scan.

Roles are assigned on the sign-in side, not in the panel. The bar also holds the environment badge, the Publish button, a light or dark theme toggle, and sign out.
